subtopic: STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION AS TO CONTINUED SUPPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION AS TO CONTINUED SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement regarding the current position of the government in relation to the national civil emergency measures program. My reason for doing so is to clarify a number of misconceptions which have been reported to me to be arising across Canada in the minds of the public, and in the government sector as well, following the general statement made in the house by my colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson), on December 7, 1967, with regard to government proposals to reduce spending in this particular area.
Since that statement the government has approved a series of recommendations arising out of a detailed study by the Canada Emergency Measures Organization. The study took into consideration intelligence regarding the threat, recent developments in scientific and technical knowledge of nuclear hazards, and the desirability of reducing federal government expenditures.
The government will continue to support this important work but with a reduced budget, a streamlined organization and improved national management and co-ordination. Greater emphasis will be placed upon the acceptance by governments at all levels of civil emergency planning as a part of day to day government activity, and even greater reliance will be placed upon the capacity of existing government services to expand and to deal with a war emergency. This is a change from former concepts which envisaged the training of large groups of volunteers as civil defence workers.
While it is the government's purpose to reduce recurring administrative and maintenance costs, it is not proposed to proceed with the wholesale dismantling of existing facilities. Major systems such as the emergency broadcasting capacity and emergency government operating centres which have been
27053-404J
developed over the past several years will be maintained, in a reduced state but in a condition that will allow their activation in short order in the event of a crisis.
Training will be limited to the necessary instruction required by officials, professionals and specialists who have been assigned to wartime responsibilities in shadow organizations.
The value of many civil emergency measures for war in peacetime disaster situation has been effectively demonstrated in Canada time and time again. While the federal government does not support emergency measures which are designed solely to meet a peacetime disaster, nevertheless it is accepted that the wartime measures we develop or assist to develop will be used to their full potential in peacetime disaster situations. Many provinces and municipalities have chosen in the past, and propose to continue in the future, to augment wartime emergency capacities with peacetime emergency programming funded entirely by themselves. The Canada Emergency Measures Organization itself has been charged by government to co-ordinate the initial federal response to any peacetime disaster situation which affects the federal government directly or in which the federal government is involved by provincial invitation, and will continue to meet that responsibility.
I have communicated the substance of our new approach to the provincial ministers responsible for civil emergency planning, together with estimates of the reduced federal financial support which will be available to assist provinces and municipalities in their emergency measures programs. Officials of the Canada Emergency Measures Organization met last week with the senior provincial officials involved from all provinces and have agreed upon the methods to be used to reduce spending in this field which at the same time will enable Canada to retain a viable national program of plans and emergency measures systems capable of rapid expansion to meet the possibility of a war which we hope will never occur.

speechtext:
think we would all agree with the last sentence in the minister's statement, that the emergency measures organization was designed to meet conditions which might arise in the event of a war which we all hope will never occur.
I believe it has been apparent for the past two or three years that the government has been anything but enthusiastic as far as the emergency measures organization is concerned, and that it has been loath to co-operate with those provinces which have felt a real need for emergency measures operations within their jurisdictions. Now apparently it intends to withdraw a considerable proportion of the funds which in the past it has put up on a cost sharing basis with the provinces and the municipalities within them.
In my personal view this is a matter for considerable regret, bearing in mind particularly that some of the provinces have felt there was a real need for the emergency measures organization. I hope the announcement does not mean that the basic federal emergency measures organization is in effect to disappear. The hon. gentleman indicated that a good deal of the support previously afforded the emergency measures organization was being withdrawn but that viable emergency measures systems would continue. In other words, on one hand we are told that the organization is to disappear and on the other we are assured it will continue. I hope the minister actually means that the basic organization will continue to exist in an effective form.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION AS TO CONTINUED SUPPORT
speechtext:
The effect of the minister's statement is that substantial reductions are to take place in the emergency measures program. I presume that if cuts in expenditures have to be made, this is one of the areas in which they could be undertaken.
However, I should like to say that I hope these cuts will not be made in such a way as to adversely affect the training of civil defence workers in specialized categories. I believe there is a great deal of support for the minister's contention that much of this civil defence work can be done by existing government services. But within these services, in the provinces and in the municipalities, there is much to be said for programs of special training.
I hope also that the government will not lose sight of the value of training federal,

DEBATES	February 6. 19S8
provincial and municipal defence workers to meet civil disasters, bearing in mind that the organization is being used increasingly for this purpose. We have suffered many times from disasters of various sorts, including flooding of the kind now being experienced in Ontario; and usually when they occur we throw some makeshift organizations into being to deal with them. An organization which could be made operative within a matter of hours through federal, provincial and municipal co-operation to meet civil disasters is something at which we in Canada should aim.
The minister told us he was making this statement because some misconceptions had arisen with respect to the emergency measures program. I hope the minister will make a statement to the house fairly soon with reference to the Canada-United States agreement on emergency measures. There has been a good deal of misunderstanding and I think some misgivings about an agreement that refers to control of manpower and personnel, and about economic controls and economic priorities. If other members have been receiving letters as I have about the interpretation which people have put on this United States-Canada agreement on emergency measures, then I think some statement from the minister would be most appropriate fairly soon.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION AS TO CONTINUED SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened very carefully to the statement made by the hon. minister with reference to his intention to reduce the funds allocated to emergency measures.
I hope, like the hon. members who spoke before me, that those cut-backs will not affect the studies or the training of civil protection staff. I know that, in a town near Ottawa, courses are given at the present time to the benefit of the mayors of municipalities, and some mayors in the province of Quebec attend those courses. I should like to see the number of civil defence schools, whose purpose is to help fight against disasters always possible in peacetime, not only maintained but increased, so that the province of Quebec too, would have a civil defence school.
I know that lately the secretary of the province met with the hon. minister. The minister said that no agreement had been reached with regard to the institution of a school in the province of Quebec, but he did not say whether or not negotiations were in
February 6, 19S8	COMMONS
progress. However, I hope that they will continue between the federal and Quebec governments so that such schools may be established in Quebec with a view to training some people to fight against disasters which may occur anywhere in our communities.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION AS TO CONTINUED SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to this page and a half of euphemisms which suggest that something that is being scrapped is not being scrapped at all. We might have wondered why cuts were being made with respect to the national civil emergency program. It was because the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue felt that any cuts made in that program would be almost invisible. If a poll had been taken on the streets it is likely that the result would have shown that people did not know what the national civil emergency organization had been doing recently, and thus the ministers assumed they could eliminate this program.
The timing is rather startling. This announcement comes when the federal government is reasserting its concern about many areas in the Canadian governmental structure, defence being one, and so it is surprising to find that civil defence can be let go so lightly. Recent developments in technical knowledge of nuclear hazards are such as to make anyone throw up his hands in horror; none the less there is much that can be done in the area of civil defence to combat those hazards.
So far as the suggestion is concerned that municipalities across the country will take up some of the slack, I would ask where we can find any municipality that would have any source of funds whatsoever for this sort of purpose, considering the financial strain the municipal level of government is under right across our country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he is now in a position to answer the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Ontario concerning Canada's role on the international control commission on Viet Nam. speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Ontario asked a series of questions regarding the current situation in Viet Nam and the Canadian government's position in that regard.
Let me first say and emphasize that his concerns are fully shared by the government. We have been following recent developments in Viet Nam with close attention on the basis of reports from our representatives in Viet Nam, in Washington and elsewhere. In the
Inquiries of the Ministry past few days our main and immediate concern has been the safety of Canadians in Viet Nam. We have neither planned nor been asked to undertake any new or different role as a result of recent events, the military and diplomatic significance of which it may take some time to assess.
As far as Canada's membership in the international control commission is concerned, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has on many occasions, both in the house and elsewhere, mentioned the concerns and frustrations we Canadians, no less than the military and civilian individuals who have served with the commission, have experienced in a very difficult assignment. At the same time the house will wish to bear in mind the fact that the international control commission is the one surviving institution formally provided for in the 1954 agreement to which both sides to the conflict maintain they would be prepared to return. This may provide in due course a basis for a new settlement.
In formulating the government's policies over the past two or three years, all these considerations have been taken into account and we cannot yet see any reason for changing them, dramatic and tragic though the events of the past few days may have been.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: In view of the answer of the minister and his observation that the government is particularly concerned with the safety of Canadians in Viet Nam, can the minister tell us whether any Canadians have actually lost their lives in Viet Nam during the events of the last week?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I think the house will recognize, communications particularly with outlying districts beyond Saigon and the principal centres have been very difficult indeed. We have been able to confirm the continuing safety of a great many Canadians, particularly those connected with the international control commission, but the safety of the remainder is still unknown. We have yet no information which would indicate that any Canadians have been killed.

The house resumed, from Monday, February 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-191, to amend the Excise Tax Act-Mr. Sharp-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening clause 11 was under discussion.
On clause 11:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as you said, when the house rose last night we were on clause 11 of this bill. I have now had an opportunity of looking into the matter raised by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and others. Perhaps I may give an explanation of the position. There is some history of representations on this matter, but I can confirm that most of them are rather out-dated. Apart from occasional references in the House of Commons I cannot find in my files any great number of representations since 1963 or 1964. However, I know the problem has been there, and I will give a short explanation of the root of the difficulty.
The Excise Tax Act provides exemption from sales tax for a comprehensive list of machinery and equipment used in farm operations. This is provided by listing certain items in part IV of schedule III of the act and also by reference to a long list of tariff items in part VII of schedule III. These tariff items, starting with item 40900-1, describe a wide range of farm machinery and equipment. The Excise Tax Act does not provide blanket exemptions for everything used on a farm or everything used in a factory. Exemptions from sales tax must be described as precisely as possible if they are to be administered fairly and efficiently. A piece of equipment

used on a farm or by farmers is not exempt from sales tax unless it is covered by the wording of the many exemptions in schedule III of the act.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The fact that exemptions are provided from a general sales tax makes it inevitable that some thin lines must be drawn in some areas between articles which are exempt and articles which are taxable. This happens in the case of machinery used for manufacturing, and it happens in the case of equipment used on farms.
To the best of my knowledge it has been the policy of successive governments since the sales tax was introduced that trucks used for transportation would be subject to sales tax. There has been an exemption for farm wagons since the early thirties, and this exemption also covered boxes for such wagons until 1956, when a tariff board decision made it necessary to add a specific exemption for boxes for farm wagons which is now in the act. The existence of this exemption for farm wagons and boxes used on farm wagons creates a borderline problem with respect to self propelled trucks which may also be used on a farm.
As the hon. member mentions, Mr. Chairman, changes in technology may have made horse drawn wagons and even four-wheeled tractor drawn wagons obsolete in some farming operations. New models and types of machines and equipment are introduced every year, and it is inevitable that the descriptions of exempt items may become out of date. The development of specialized trucks and specialized loading and unloading devices for such trucks has brought into use new items of equipment which do not qualify under the existing exemptions.
It has been suggested that the fact that tariff item 40924-1, which is listed with the exemptions, refers to "all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery n.o.p.," is a statement of intention on the part of the Department of Finance that all forms of machinery used in agriculture are meant to be exempt from sales tax. This is certainly not my view and I believe it has not been the view of any previous minister of finance. It is possible that the technology of farming operations has moved beyond the wording and even the intention of the existing exemptions and, as I promised last night, I will certainly undertake to give careful consideration to representations that particular classes of farm machinery be added to the list of exemptions.
February 6, 19G8

However, I think hope should not be entertained that there is any chance of motor trucks used on farms being made exempt, and much more information would be required before I could express any view about the possibility of exempting special boxes or mechanical devices for use with such trucks.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister for the trouble he has gone to in order to give us this explanation. I do not think there is any disagreement between what he has said and what we have tried to put forward. We agree that there has been a long history to this argument, if you wish to call it that.
We believe, Mr. Chairman, that the difficulty arises over the confusion in terms. This was the reason that last night we asked the minister to give a definition of what he meant by "wagon". We still cannot understand why he is putting through a piece of legislation for which he expects our support when he is unable to explain to the committee the meaning of the term "wagon" used in the legislation.
I have searched for and found a legal definition of the term "wagon" that would be quite acceptable to me. It is in an act that was passed by parliament in 1930, I believe, and can be found at page 694 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, volume I. I refer to what is commonly known as the Canada Grain Act. Wagon is defined under paragraph (27) of section 2 as follows:
"wagon" means any vehicle to deliver grain to a country elevator.
I said last night, Mr. Chairman, that our difficulty arose when we went to one of the departments to find out what was meant by these items that are listed under tariff item 409f to which the minister has referred. For example, there is the item "gravity discharge farm wagon boxes". I am not talking about trucks.
In this regard I should like to quote some of the correspondence I had with the deputy minister of national revenue in 1961. As I said before, I think this is where the confusion in terms arises. In the letter he wrote to me the deputy minister said in part:
Being precluded from entry under item 409f, two provisions remain for consideration in classifying the truck bodies in question-
Excise Tax Act
The minister refers to "truck bodies", and we are talking about truck boxes. There is a big difference. The letter continues:
-tariff item 446a, the "basket" provision covering manufactures of iron or steel and tariff item 438f relating to parts for motor vehicles. The latter item, in my opinion, more specifically describes these truck bodies.
We are not talking about truck bodies but about truck boxes. In view of the legal definition given by the Department of Justice of the government of Canada, we cannot understand why wagon boxes are exempt but not truck boxes. Under the definition of "wagon" in the Canada Grain Act trucks would also be exempt, but we are not going that far in asking the minister to explain what he means by "wagon".
I dealt further with this question with the deputy minister of the day, and in one of my letters I had this to say:
Item 438f deals with parts of motor vehicles. I contend that a steel truck, grain or livestock box is not part of what is considered a motor vehicle or the chassis thereof, but rather an article to be mounted or attached thereto. Item 438a states such articles shall be valued separately, and duty assessed under tariff items regularly applicable thereto.
In western Canada, and the same may be said of eastern Canada, automotive dealers very seldom sell a farm truck or vehicle with steel grain box attached. If the farmer requires a grain box the normal procedure is for the farmer, or dealer, to obtain one from an implement dealer. Grain and livestock truck boxes are usually manufactured by those specialized in manufacturing agricultural implements and not from automotive manufacturers.
That is the point I am trying to get across, Mr. Chairman.
Most automotive dealers price sheets list chassis only and do not include a price for a grain or livestock box. Therefore, I contend a grain box should not be considered as a part of the truck or vehicle but considered under some other heading.
I say it should be considered under the heading in tariff item 409f of a gravity discharge farm wagon box or, as I said before, as all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery n.o.p.-not otherwise provided for.
To continue with my letter:
I further contend a steel grain or stock truck box could be included under the heading of agriculture implements for the following reasons. In legal dictionaries, the term implement is defined as a thing of necessary use in any trade. The word necessary is defined as those things to the doing of a thing which are reasonably required.
I have gone through some dictionaries to find a definition of "truck box" or "wagon box" that the department would accept. I

comes with a wagon or truck should be defined as being a farm implement. The question may be asked, what do we mean by a wagon? If we do not accept the truck chassis in this definition will we accept the definition in the Canada Grain Act?
As I said, I have had a lot of correspondence on this subject and I have some here with the first minister of finance with whom I dealt. He happened to be a member of my own party, and I admit that I got about as far with him as I have got with the present minister. I do not blame the ministers so much as the officials of the department who occupy their positions for periods of years. They know that these questions have been raised not only by myself but by other hon. members such as the hon. member for Springfield. They must have heard these questions raised by dozens of members. Many western members have made substantial representations on the points I am trying to raise.
I regret that the machinery does not seem to exist whereby we can bring to the minister's attention the points we are driving at. He asked why did I not go to see him when his door was open to hon. members? We have done this but it has been to no avail. We now intend to get from the minister, if possible, a definition of "farm wagon."
I referred to the first representation I made to the minister of finance I originally dealt with. I was dealing with the item I am dealing with here, truck boxes which are brought to Canada from the United States, and I said in that letter:
I understand a similar request was made some time ago, but was refused on the grounds that although similar boxes were not made in Canada, they could be if the market warranted production. I do not disagree with the decision that was made at that time. Although I am a westerner, I am one who believes we must protect Canadian industry where possible, provided it does not create too heavy a burden on some other section of our country. Your previous decision gave Canadian industry an opportunity to take advantage of any potential Canadian market. Through lack of aggression, or some other reason, our industry has apparently not seen fit to take advantage of the opportunity afforded to them by your action.
At the present time, in certain areas of the prairie provinces, there is a demand for a light steel grain and livestock truck box. The farmers have been unable to obtain them in Canada, at least from recognized manufacturers of this type of farm equipment. Some may be manufactured locally in some areas of the west.
On investigation by some western manufacturers to provide this market with the product in demand, it was found that their source of supply could not produce the strong high tensile steel required, all other types of steel were too heavy for practical use.
Excise Tax Act
Anticipating a question which you might logically ask as to whether some substitute Canadian material could not be used, I will list some of the reasons the farmer is now demanding this type of steel box:-
I ask the minister whether a high tensile steel box may be included as a part. I continue:
- (a) Previous steel boxes on the market have been too heavy to be handled manually on the farm.
(b)	With the advent of a greater demand for stock most western farmers now raise cattle as well as grain on their farms. Both must be hauled to market. A steel box can be washed out quickly and thoroughly after hauling cattle and be ready for grain immediately.
(c)	Most western farms are now fully mechanized and many farmers haul their own fuel. Any spillage can be easily washed from steel and will not soak into the platform as it does on a wooden base.
Western farmers want the steel box. I mentioned some of these matters last night. I continue reading:
(d)	Treated wheat-
I am referring to poisoned wheat.
-used for seeding purposes can be handled in a steel box with fewer precautions than in a wooden one.
That is reasonable.
All my efforts to date to convince the excise branch there are at present ample listings under their tariff regufations to allow entry of such a box have not been fruitful. They insist direction must come from your department, spelling out in detail the nature of the box required before they will rule duty free for the farmers.
I have been unable to convince them that the steel grain box could be included under the heading of agricultural implement.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I have mentioned a number of these definitions. What this situation simply means to the western farmer is that at present there is a 25 per cent duty on these boxes plus an 11 per cent sales tax. The result is that for every $1,000 farmers spend on them at least $400 goes to the government. The minister has been out west. He says he understands the plight of the western farmer who finds himself caught in the cost-price squeeze. It seems odd to me that since these boxes are now essential to farm operations they should not be exempt from tax.
I point out once again that we are not asking for an exemption for trucks. If we were I would expect the minister to tell us that an end-use certificate should be given. Farmers would have no objection to giving end-use certificates with regard to trucks

February 6, 1968
Excise Tax Act
because it is admitted they can be used for other purposes. Nevertheless, 99 times out of 100 the farmers who buy them use them exclusively for farm purposes. All we are asking the hon. gentleman to do is to define what he means by "wagon". Will he not accept that it is the same thing as a truck?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I begin by saying that in so far as hon. members are making representation for a change in the law their comments will be taken into consideration when amendments are next made to the legislation.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has asked me on what basis the Department of National Revenue now defines a farm wagon. I will give him a direct answer. It may not satisfy him but I will try to be as clear as I can. The consistent policy in administering this statutory provision has been to accept the ordinary dictionary definition of the term "wagon" and regard as entitled to the benefits of the exemption those farm wagons equipped with four wheels. Accordingly, as a farm wagon is a general purpose implement useful in performing a large number of functions the following definition, taken from Funk and Wagnalls New Standard Dictionary of the English Language, the same dictionary as the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek used, is followed by the department in administering this exempting provision:
A four-wheeled vehicle having a rectangular boxlike body, complete with tongue, designed to be horse drawn.
It has been the policy of the department to regard all four-wheeled wagons, whether horse or tractor drawn, designed for farm application, with or without box, to be unconditionally exempt from sales tax under the abovementioned statutory provision. This means that two-wheeled vehicles, for example, trailers, cannot qualify for exemption.
Similarly, exemption from sales tax is provided in item 4 of part IV of the Excise Tax Act, under the heading "Farm and Forest", for the following goods:
Boxes for farm wagons, and article and materials for use exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
There have been numerous requests over the years for exemption from sales tax for boxes for farm trucks, but these have been ruled to be subject to sales tax at the current rate since the Excise Tax Act as at present enacted makes no provision for their exemption.

I should like to thank the minister for giving us those definitions in relation to farm wagons and wagon boxes. The subject under consideration here really is the attitude of the government or the attitude of the Department of National Revenue toward the whole question of the tax placed on some of these items. Taking a political view of these things, we all know that the boast has been made across Canada that excise taxes and tariffs have been removed from farm machinery. We also know that certain items are exempt from taxation when a certificate is signed to the effect that their use will be restricted to the farm. Air-cooled engines and generating plants come into this category. The guide line in the mind of the average farmer is, therefore, that provided an article is to be used solely for agricultural purposes parliament has intended that it be exempt from tax.
This is the feeling today in connection with truck boxes. The attitude of the department has in my opinion been archaic. The rulings have departed from the intention of parliament that boxes for wagons should be exempt. Today the truck has taken the place of the wagon, and in these circumstances a great deal of dissatisfaction exists in connection with the stand now taken by the department.
With regard to clause 11, I congratulate the minister and the government for having made an exemption to cover parts. I know this will be welcomed by farmers not only in connection with farm wagons but in connection with a number of other items.
We should like to see the minister bring this act up to date. Let him not delay doing so until some time in the distant future, as seems to be the tendency of all ministers of finance. In practice, ministers of that department never stay in office long enough to do anything about these things. We do not know how much longer the present minister will be holding the portfolio of finance. Maybe he will have other duties within a short period of time. We should like him to achieve this major step on behalf of our farmers with the least possible delay, in keeping with the boast made by his party that it has removed tariffs from farm equipment.

I rise to support the
representations made by my hon. friend from Swift Current-Maple Creek with respect to this matter. I must compliment him on his presentation. He has certainly done his homework, and there is little I can add to what he
February 6, 1968

has said. He spoke for most farmers across Canada and particularly for those in the west.
My hon. friend from Rosthern who has just resumed his seat put his finger on an anomalous situation when he pointed out that the definition used in connection with farm wagons applied some 25 or 30 years ago. How many people are using the old-fashioned wagon box today? A truck box on an automated vehicle has taken its place. Consequently the definition to which the minister referred is outmoded and ought no longer to be used. I support entirely what my hon. friends have said on this point. It is high time the minister and his officials updated the legislation with respect to farm boxes.

I, too, would like to say a few words in support of the representations which my hon. friend from Swift Current-Maple Creek has just finished making in the course of his well prepared statement on this issue. The very fact that farm wagons are now being defined as fourwheeled farm wagons equipped to be tractor drawn is an indication that the act is more than 30 years out of date. I doubt that half of one per cent of the farms in western Canada use a wagon of any type today. Most farms have one or two large farm trucks. I do not think the minister should have any hesitation in recognizing that we are living in 1968 and that everything rolls on rubber and is motorized.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In those earlier days combines were few in number. Today everyone has a combine and a good many of them are self-propelled. Farm trucks are also self-propelled. The province of Saskatchewan recognized the importance of farm trucks when it passed legislation a year ago exempting fuel used by those trucks, when used on farms, from tax. I think the minister should take a personal interest in this matter and see to it that farm truck boxes are exempted from this tax.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to join with my prairie colleagues in thanking the minister for his undertaking to consider in the next short while the possibility of further revising the Excise Tax Act and the regulations, so as to exempt farm truck boxes from this tax. As I indicated last night, and as other hon. members have indicated, it is difficult to understand how a quarter of a century can pass before the law is updated to present-day reality. We have all heard the old saying, which I think comes from "Oliver
Excise Tax Act
Twist," that in some respects the law is an ass. Here we have a perfect example of that. It is inconceivable that there can be much hesitation in changing the Excise Tax Act in this respect. Last night the Minister of National Revenue said that on many occasions genuine efforts have been made to attempt to meet the legitimate requests of western farmers. This is a good opportunity to put such a sentiment into effect by changing this act to reflect modern conditions on Canadian farms.
I do not suppose much would be gained by prolonging this debate inasmuch as the minister has given a clearcut undertaking that he will examine this matter in detail. I take him to mean that before the passage of more than four or five months we will be hearing from him specifically in this connection.

Mr. Chairman, now that the problem regarding the definition of farm wagons seems to be settled, I should like to direct a question to the hon. minister.
I shall not take much of the time of the house, but farm wagons and particularly their parts are still of interest to me, since I come from eastern Canada. We are all aware of the tax added to the price of the wagons made in Canada. If farm wagons or their parts were made in the United States, would the customs duty still be charged or would it disappear along with the taxes, as provided by the clause now under consideration?

I would like to draw the minister's attention to a few remarks he made last night, as recorded on page 6398 of Hansard. He said:
It was in response to representations that the words "and parts thereof" have been added. It is a relieving section which does not add any tax. It relieves parts of farm wagons and sleds from the tax, and I am sure the hon. gentleman would not want to oppose that.
We are not opposing that, but we want the minister to include farm truck boxes and we maintain that all he has to do is add a few words to clause 11.
Hon. members will recall that when the minister read the definition taken by the department from Funk and Wagnall, the dictionary the legal branch uses, he mentioned "horse drawn vehicle," but apparently the department has changed the dictionary definition because the bill reads, "to be tractor drawn." This confirms our argument that a farm truck box is a wagon drawn by a truck.

February 6, 1968
Excise Tax Act
I am sure the minister, to use his own words, would not want to oppose such a change, knowing the position of the farmers in western Canada.
I could make a long speech about the government's railway line abandonment policy, as a result of which trucks with large, light steel boxes are more essential to farmers now than ever before. They have to haul their grain longer distances and these boxes must be light in order to carry large quantities of grain. Otherwise the cost factor would become prohibitive, and if the cost of production is too high farmers in many areas will not be able to grow grain. I do not want to suggest exact words to the minister but he could include the phrase, "or truck drawn." I am sure he realizes what we want. We want steel truck boxes exempted. They are not made by automotive manufacturers but by farm machinery manufacturers.
With respect to the minister's statement that representations had been made to him, I would like to know how they were made. As I told him, I have been making representations on this subject ever since 1961 and I do not think I have missed a single year. Last night the Minister of National Revenue made light of the fact that we had not brought up this matter previously. I would refer him to volume 3 of 1963 Hansard, July 25, when the matter was raised with the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport.
On July 30 of that year the matter was raised again, as recorded on pages 2649 and 2650 of Hansard. I also refer the minister to pages 2796, 2806, to 2808, and 2811 to 2815. On one occasion I had a private bill before the house titled "Bureaucratic Oppression," which drew attention to the fact that we could not get a definition from either department because they would not agree. They would not even accept the definition in the Canada Grain Act, a legal statute passed by parliament. What will they accept? The minister should make it perfectly clear what he means by a wagon and whether it includes truck boxes. When he includes the words "to be tractor drawn" he admits in effect that this is different from the definition in Funk and Wagnall which refers to a horse-drawn vehicle.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to make a few remarks on the budgetary legislation before us I want to assure the minister that I have no intention or desire to add to the already heavy burden resting upon his shoulders as Minister of Finance. The fact that the greater part of his burden has to do with the minister's interest in the future of his party, rather than in the economy of Canada, does not alter the situation that today we believe he is a sorely tried man.
The minister probably feels that he should be somewhere else today listening to more important things, but we in the house have to deal with this legislation which all of us consider to be vitally important to Canadians as a whole. So it is purely in a spirit of helpfulness that I wish to advance some ideas on the general subject of the national economy and in particular what I believe to be serious shortcomings in the approach of the Minister of Finance and the government as a whole to our economic problems.
This legislation is designed to implement what has been called a mini-budget, an emergency measure which I feel was forced upon the minister and the government by their own bungling. In view of the minister's statements of the past few years as to the state of the economy and the adequacy of his own policies, I would refer to this interim budget as an alibi budget for those statements and legislation, designed to excuse and correct the minister's grievous errors in policies and his gross miscalculations.

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
According to the minister's explanation earlier, his aim in this legislation is to fight inflation. He seeks by these and other proposals to put the brakes on the Canadian economy. I submit that the prime target of his anti-inflationary tactics is the little man, the average taxpayer, the ordinary Canadian, the most put upon, overburdened and exploited unit in our tax system. The minister also had a few pious words of advice for labour and private enterprise. He cautioned them to go slow, cut back and show restraint, and there have been some violent reactions to his suggestions from both labour and industry.
So far the minister has done nothing but speak about one of the principal areas where effective anti-inflationary action might be taken, namely, excessive government spending, and right now government spending is up by 15 per cent. The minister's forecast is for an increase of 4.5 per cent in government expenditure this year, in spite of the so-called cutbacks which in fact were only propaganda. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this figure is also misleading. It does not take into account the money required for the government medicare scheme due to be launched on July 1, although that date has not yet been announced in parliament as the definite date for the implementation of this scheme. This appears to be a classic case of the old saying: Do as I say, not as I do.
As I have said, I can appreciate the minister's difficult position. Surely it must be exceedingly difficult for him to bring himself to consider today such routine matters as the nation's economy. In fact, this must have been the case starting two weeks ago and will in all likelihood continue to be so until next April 5.
The minister has never been one to show reluctance in giving his own ideas and solutions first place as the only answers to the economic problems of Canada. I have observed that he has shown a degree of selfconfidence which in another minister might be mistaken for arrogance but which he knows so well how to project. It is not too much to say that the Minister of Finance has demonstrated a faith in his own infallibility which few of us possess. I wonder whether the minister has ever considered the possibility that his ideas and projections might be wrong. Has he ever taken the time to consider other views, new theories, fresh policies and, most important, the experience of other countries in similar situations and what they
February 6, 1968

have been able to accomplish or to attempt in establishing new policies? Surely even the minister must realize how damaging it would be, not only to the national economy but to his political ambitions, if it turned out that he had pursued the wrong policies and had applied incorrect measures.
I wonder whether the minister has ever heard of Edward Holloway. Edward Holloway is the honorary secretary of the economic research council of Great Britain. He is also the director of Commonwealth Industries Association Limited. One of Mr. Holloway's organizations has recently completed the first part of a research program specifically devoted to finding the prime source of Great Britain's continuing inflation. This program is called the national recovery program. It was undertaken following the publication last year of a manifesto drawn up by 19 leading economists, industrialists and writers in Great Britain. They include such celebrated persons as Professor C. Northcote Parkinson, the father of Parkinson's law with the application of which, particularly in such government ministries as the Department of Finance, I am sure the minister is familiar. This manifesto aroused such interest that funds were soon forthcoming for the exhaustive and detailed study of inflation and its prime cause.
So far the findings have been revolutionary, to say the least. They are of a standard and importance which I would have thought sufficient to command the attention of the minister and the government and, indeed, of all responsible members of parliament. When one considers our close and vital economic links with Great Britain, the amount of attention given to recent economic events there, and the tremendous effect such events have on our economy, it seems reasonable to assume that Canada's Minister of Finance and Canada's government would be almost as well briefed on developments in Great Britain as the British authorities themselves. Perhaps this is the case. I hope it is because if these preliminary findings in Great Britain are correct it means that the Minister of Finance and the government of Canada are carrying out the wrong policies, victimizing the wrong people, and casting the blame for inflation upon groups which may be entirely blameless, namely, organized labour, ordinary consumers, and private business.
The British research report states that inflation is not caused by a too rapid increase
Income Tax Act
in wages, is not worsened by full employment, is not reinforced by the activity of private enterprise, and is not even directly caused by government spending or budgetary deficits. The prime source of inflation, according to the researchers, is the financing of an over-all deficit in the central government's accounts by an uncontrolled creation of new money. The dominating word in this explanation is "uncontrolled". If this statement and the findings of the research group are true, it means that some of the present measures advocated both by the British government and by our own government in Canada are not only ineffective but totally wrong.
One of the most significant findings of the group in Britain is that when public spending rises faster than private spending there is a progressive slowing down in industrial growth. The sparkplug of a nation's economy is the private sector. What they have found is that various governments faced with economic difficulties such as inflation have taken money out of the private sector so as to reduce demand but at the same time have increased the money supply by the same amount or more to sustain a high rate of public spending. This means that for all practical purposes total demand has not been reduced at all.
The vital factor in this approach is that while the government has increased the money supply and failed to reduce its own spending, it has forced cut-backs in spending in the private sector and thus put the brake on industrial production. Inevitably this increases the inflationary pressure and leads to an aggravation of the very condition they have sought to cure. They have added to the money supply but reduced industrial output. In so doing they have attracted unnecessary imports and hobbled exports. Increased public spending and an increase in money are no substitute for production from an active private sector. Governments cannot spend their way out of recession, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The basis for the findings in the report is that the nation's total demand for goods and services is always satisfied by the nation's own production plus imports. When production slows down within the country the pressure for imports grows; when internal production picks up this import pressure declines.
The report further states that its preliminary findings strongly indicate that the proper way to gain a favourable balance of trade

February 6, 1968
Income Tax Act
and all the economic benefits that go with this is to allow total demand, and particularly consumer demand, to grow. The private sector, rather than being restricted and hampered, should be allowed and encouraged to go ahead full blast. This obviously is just the opposite course to that upon which the government and the Minister of Finance are now embarked.
I am not an economist, nor have I ever pretended to be. As a result I cannot say whether or not all these things are true. But I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that because of their apparent good sense and the sound credentials of their authors these findings are at least worthy of the government's serious attention. These findings and recommendations are very similar to those urged upon the government by organized labour in this country.
The key to the findings in the British report is that inflation can be shut off at the source if the central government will only act to control its own spending in relation to the money supply. The over-all difference between government income and expenditure must be financed by genuine borrowing, sale of government securities, and by genuine saving, always undertaken in relation to the creation of new money. Such responsible government action would mean that consumer demand could be encouraged instead of dampened down. Wage increases could be tolerated at a reasonable level of annual growth and private enterprise could free itself from government restrictions and expand its own rate of economic growth. The mistake has been to try to manage demand instead of managing the money supply.
Lord Cromer, when still governor of the Bank of England, said that Britain had a system whereby exchequer financing led to "the creation of money quasi-automatically". This may be, for different reasons perhaps, the situation here in Canada. It is well within the power of the government to control the money supply. If the findings of the British researchers are correct, then it is not only an obligation but a vital necessity for the minister and his officials to re-examine their policies and proposals in this fight.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I am not an economist, but I admit that as a layman I have been impressed by all the implications of these latest findings by these British researchers. I do not believe that they can be dismissed lightly as being from another country or as dealing with different conditions.

Generally speaking, all the western nations face roughly the same economic problems within the context of roughly similar systems.
I sincerely believe that much good for Canada would come out of a close study of this matter by the minister and his departmental officials. It seems to me that in a country as prosperous, as dynamic and as promising as Canada there is something fundamentally wrong with a system that inhibits business initiative and victimizes our working people as the only way to cure our economic problems.
In a few months the name of the minister may become a household word in Canada for reasons other than economic. I would pose this question to him: How much prouder would he be, how much more lasting his fame, if the history books could record that he was the first to break through the restrictive barriers of old economic practice into the green fields of stable and equitable prosperity for Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the previous speaker on his address and to commend it to the officials of the Department of Finance as worthy of consideration. I too am surprised that the department has brought forward in this bill the same type of legislation that has been introduced on numerous occasions and as a result of which the little man has to pay the penalty for economic conditions over which he has absolutely no control. Workers ask for more money so they can continue to pay the rent. They do not ask for money in anticipation of the rent going up because rents are continually going up. It is often argued in negotiations with organized labour that as soon as wage increases are granted rents seem to rise. Workers who are not members of organized labour discover that even in the absence of a wage increase their rents go up just the same. They really have no control over this problem.
In introducing the budget resolution to bring about the income tax amendments now before the house the minister indicated that one of his prime aims was to assist in halting inflation. I agree with this. I do not subscribe to the argument that the way to end inflation is to curtail government spending. I do not agree that it is necessary to curtail certain spending. Cut-backs in housebuilding are not the way to curtail inflation in this nation. According to this morning's Montreal Gazette there are something like 75,000 unemployed
February 6, 19B8

in that city, many of them carpenters, electricians and members of the building trades. It seems to me that this is not the way to curb inflation. In this specific instance the minister has decided to impose a 5 per cent income tax surcharge with a ceiling of $600. Again this is making the little people pay the same as those at the top of the scale.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I know that the minister has been a civil servant and that he is probably closer to the establishment than most ministers of finance have been. He was part of it and knew its inner workings. I think the establishment in Ottawa lives in an ivory tower. They are willing to tax the little people of Canada, those in the lower income bracket, but they always put a ceiling on the effective income to be taxed because they do not want those who have high incomes to pay heavy taxes.
I remember the arguments about old age security and about cutting off assistance at $60 a month, and so on. The government then paid $90 and it has bumped that figure up to $120. I ask, why should those who have been able to make their mark in society not help those who have not done so well? Why should the little man not receive some benefit? Perhaps the executive types who live in the lofty, refined atmosphere of the Rideau Club do not know what is happening today. I suspect they do.
The Carter commission says that one way to raise tax money is to tax the mining industry. I come from an area where there is much mining. Many of the early mines of Canada are in the area I represent. As a result I have always been interested in the propaganda that the mines have put out. Though some mines make colossal profits the mining industry as a whole has always been loudest in shouting to the establishment when new taxes are proposed, "Don't rock the boat." Carter said that there was no justification for the mining exemption and I do not think that a three-year tax exemption should be allowed for the mines.
Many members of this house may have made or lost money on Texas Gulf. Some of them may have made or lost money on adjacent mines such as Windfall and others.
How did you do?

Recently an article appeared in the Timmins Press which indicated that Texas Gulf will make a tax free profit for the next three years of $400,000 per day. I know 27053-405

International Nickel enjoys the same type of exemption completely without justification. I see no logic in extending a tax exemption in those circumstances.
When we talk about exemptions for individuals the story is different. Exemptions for individuals these days ought to be on the basis of $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married couples. The government will not increase the exemptions but is increasing taxes. For the value of the exemption to keep pace with the inflated value of our dollar I

February 6. 1968
Income Tax Act
submit that single persons ought to be granted a $1,500 exemption. The $1,000 that parliament granted 20 years ago is probably worth less than $500 in real terms today. Perhaps $2,000 as the exemption for single persons would be more realistic. It would be just enough to enable an individual to maintain the standard of living he enjoyed 20 years ago.
Of course, we are always willing to put a ceiling on taxes. Those in the high income bracket will not need to pay more than $600 in additional taxes, the reason being that the establishment does not want the big people in this country to get hurt. When it comes to the little man the story is different. Most of our people are little people. I represent a constituency whose people will be paying extra taxes, which will hurt their purchasing power. The little man is at the bottom of the totem pole and the little man will have his standard of living lowered by increased taxes. The establishment's idea is that by lowering the purchasing power of the little man at the bottom of the totem pole a large number of people will have less money to spend and inflation will be curbed. Of course, in simple terms we are lowering the standard of living of the little man, and we should not do that.
I do not expect the establishment to agree to changes that will hurt their friends, but sooner or later members of parliament will have to make a decision. They will have to go out on the hustings, face those who will be paying less than $600 a year extra and explain to them why the per cent surcharge has been imposed. The government will not be influenced by my remarks but I know that the establishment will have much explaining to do in the next election because candidates from every political party will be asked by the electors why the extra tax was added. As I said, instead of granting increased exemptions the government is adding extra taxes. What the government should be doing is bringing the exemption into line with the reduced purchasing power of the dollar. If we look at the dollar of 20 years ago and remember that the exemption then was $1,000 for a single man, is it not common sense to just about double the exemption to take care of today's inflated dollar? The people at the bottom of the totem pole who outnumber those higher up

are the ones who are asked to make sacrifices, who are asked to lower their standard of living in the name of curbing inflation. Those at the top level will not be affected nearly as much.

the form sent out a year earlier, I am at a loss to understand what he means by simplification. According to the legal dictionary he uses, it must mean complication. Most of them are spending their limited incomes on rent, clothing, food and medical expenses. Any increase in the cost of any of these commodities or services as a result of inflation means a cut-back for them. These people must find cheaper accommodation, wear their clothing longer or eat less. Usually such cutbacks occur in respect of food. I think an increase in exemptions for these people is justified and could be a useful tool in the fight

against the evils of inflation. I am personally aware of a number of people in my own area who have been forced to sell their homes in order to carry on through the home-stretch of their lives. This is a pernicious situation.

This is not good enough in a country developing as rapidly as ours is today,

both in industry and private life, and when there is a great change from a rural to an urban economy.
The government is now coming forward and asking for an increase in the income tax. There is nothing in their program to help the municipalities which are faced with the greatest tax increase in the entire history of this country. Let us also consider another factor, the rising cost of living which continues to increase despite the appointment of a minister of the crown in charge of consumer and corporate affairs. When I asked the minister whether his department was going to study the effects of the rising interest rates he denied that his department was charged with that responsibility. If that is so, then why was the department set up if not to take into consideration one of the most important factors in the economic life of our country?
Let us face the fact that the effect of the government's actions has been to reduce the productivity of our nation and of our workers at a time when our products face great competition in world markets. What hope is there for the Canadian people when we have a government such as the present one? This is one of the reasons why we on this side of the house cannot help but condemn the government for the actions they have taken and, what is more important, for what they have not done in the face of these problems. It cannot be said that the government lacked advice. They have hired everyone in Canada they could to help them set up these little empires.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner hour I was dealing with some of the phenomena that have taken place during the last three years that finally brought about the chaotic financial position in which the government finds itself today. During the past two years in particular there has been an increasingly severe trend toward increased taxation.
We have before us at the present time a bill introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to increase income taxes. This has become necessary because of the problems now facing the nation, such as inflation, the rising cost of living, receding productivity and the increasing burden of government itself.
This takes me back to the days before this government came into office, when parliament and the Canadian people were being told how to restore Canada's position in the world and our economy at home. According to a report before me from the Ottawa Citizen of April 20, 1963 the Liberals set out seven ways to restore Canada's position in the world. The first of these was to demonstrate that Canada has a strong government at home. In view of what has happened during the last two or three years in particular, and the groping that we have seen from the finance portfolio of this government, it is interesting to reflect on this headline and to wonder as to the substance for this sort of report. I suggest that one of the reasons this measure is before us tonight is that once again the government is seeking additional money to replace money it has misspent, frittered away. It is in this position not only because of the things it did but because of the things it did not do.
The headline in the Ottawa Journal for February 12, 1963 reads "Grits want more government projects", which according to the Journal are to be at no cost to taxpayers. The article goes on to say that-
-the national council of the Liberal federation came out straight for more government sponsored projects to ease unemployment, more aid to municipalities, loans, an enlarged Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-

February 6, 1968

We are sent to parliament to try to obtain a better life for our people. We are sent here to enable our people to utilize all the resources of this country. I realize, as does every other member of the House of Commons, that government must tax in order to provide services that are necessary for our people. Nevertheless it is generally understood throughout the length and breadth of this country that certain matters can be dispensed with, that certain items add to the cost of government and raise the cost of living of our citizens.
Before the dinner adjournment I spoke of two factors that had contributed most to our present labour unrest. And, Mr. Speaker, we have labour unrest in this country because of what this government has done. The increases in income tax the government is proposing to levy will have the effect of making labour seek higher wages. This will mean an increasingly rapid upward spiral in our cost of living, and that is why I question the government's wisdom in bringing forward this measure-because it steals something from the man who carries a dinner pail. This measure will force prices up to the extent that many commodities will be out of reach of the ordinary citizens of this country.
Realizing all this, members of the opposition of the House of Commons have lost confidence in the government, as have the businessmen of this country.

The few measures the government has put forward do not come to grips with the problems that face this nation. I think that raising income taxes for our citizens is wrong; that will not achieve the purpose the government intended to achieve. This measure will have serious consequences for the future of our nation and instead of helping to solve our problems will accentuate them and make their solution more difficult. That is the bleak prospect that faces us today! No matter which government is in office, whether it be this government or some other! the problems of our nation must be faced and solved, and they will not be solved by measures such as this.
Just take a look at the decisions made by this government and at the results of those decisions. Today we have the highest cost of living in Canada's history; today the government is proposing income tax increases; today the government, through its actions, is whittling away the supply of money that is necessary to provide the houses and other essential
Income Tax Act
commodities of this country. When the Minister of Finance says that by removing the interest rate ceiling there will be a bountiful supply of money for housing I just ask him, whether any banker in his right mind would tie up his bank's money in housing for 30 years when the bank can go after more lucrative business? I submit that this government measure is wrong because it is based on a false economic premise.
Look at the mounting costs of government in this country, Mr. Speaker, and at the little empires within the government that are being built up. Nevertheless we were told in this house not long ago that the government would effect savings in government spending. The government said it would not spend as much money as it had intended spending. All I can say is that the government has proposed too little too late. It has not even begun to touch the problems that face our nation. I regret to say this, but what the government is doing will be bad for Canada; and I do not think many of our people would quarrel with what I say. I hope the government once in a while will listen to members of the opposition and to its own backbenchers. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up too much of the time of the house. However, like my friend from Rosthem (Mr. Nasserden), I cannot miss this opportunity to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) how unpopular is his present proposal in the eyes of the average retired citizens who live on a fixed income.
Factory workers were certainly expecting something other than the present tax increase proposed by the Minister of Finance. On the contrary, being practical, they were expecting the government to announce, through the Minister of Finance, a decrease in its extravagant expenditures and restraint also in the employment of civil servants whose numbers seem to be increasing at an alarming rate every month.
But, instead of that, the hon. minister announces a tax increase. Moreover, he tells us that he will have to impose another tax in a few months.

February 6, 1968
Income Tax Act
It is very difficult for the father of a family to make ends meet at the end of the year because, on one hand, the average worker must face an ever-increasing cost of living, the highest cost of living in all the history of our country and, on the other hand, he also must cope with an income tax increase, with the comforting thought that perhaps, in a few months, he will have to pay out more as a result of greater deductions which will be made on his pay check every week.
As my hon. friend from Rosthern mentioned, the hon. minister should pay attention instead to the warnings given by this side of the house and by his Liberal colleagues who surely, in private of course, warned him that he could not continue, as he has done to date, to add to the difficulties of the middle-class worker. The young man who plans to build his own home is faced with innumerable difficulties. Yesterday, I saw in a newspaper that, in the province of Quebec alone, building costs have gone up by 28 per cent. That is due to the continuous increase of income taxes and also of taxes on building materials.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
On various occasions, we have attempted to convince the hon. minister that, instead of raising taxes, he should rather endeavour to reduce them, but he has remained deaf to our appeals. It is somewhat as if we were pouring water on the back of a duck.
I referred earlier to what is in store for our retired people who have to provide for themselves with an income which has not changed for several years. Those citizens have now reached the age where they cannot find work to increase their income. From one week to the next, from one month to the next, they find it increasingly difficult to satisfy their needs.
In that respect, I have here a letter signed by Mr. Hubert Lecours, president of the national association of retired federal civil servants, Quebec section, which reads as follows:
Sir,
At a recent meeting, X was asked to tell you how we feel about the freezing of pensions to retired civil servants.
We protest vigorously against that decision taken by the government which is not only unfair but revolting and unacceptable in the present economic and economic conditions.
We would appreciate it very much if you would second the efforts of the Prime Minister who has promised a review of that shameful and undignified decision in the very near future.
Counting on your support, I remain, yours sincerely.

Before concluding, I would like to intercede on behalf of pensioners and superannuated civil servants whose revenue has not changed for many years. I would ask the Minister of Finance to see to it that these retired people, these deserving employees, who devoted the best part of their life to the welfare of their fellow-citizens, enjoy a pension enabling them to meet their present obligations. The minister should show more concern for superannuated civil servants who can hardly make both ends meet to-day. In doing this he would please not only those citizens, but also some members on both sides of the house.
Therefore, I ask the hon. minister to take steps to put an end to these continual tax increases and, on the other hand, to give a little more attention to retired civil servants.
