I listened with interest to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) and I am surprised he would criticize this bill to such an extent without criticizing it for the reasons for which it deserves criticism.
I notice he made profuse reference to editorials from various newspapers, the Toronto Star in particular, and I suppose it is because he used these newspapers as his advisors that he criticized this bill for the wrong reasons. I too take advantage of these editorials but I use them in the opposite way; whenever I am in doubt about a certain issue I read the editorials, and I find that if I do exactly the opposite to what they advise I come out right pretty well 100 per cent of the time.
I agree there is lack of confidence in the government. There is a conference in progress now, designed to renew the confidence of the Canadian people in the Liberal party and in this parliament. I am surprised the government cannot instil this confidence. After all, they have been in the confidence racket all their lives and have been quite successful at it.
There is a saying in my riding of Sudbury that only poor people can enjoy poverty. This is true; and this bill is designed to ensure that these people shall have more enjoyment than they have ever had in their lives. I think it is the most dastardly piece of legislation I have seen in my short stay of six months in this house. The minister proposes to tax those who have least ability to pay. In one clause the tax is cut off at the $600 limit. I am not a mathematician but I think a man would
February 6, 1968

arrive at this position when he is earning $28,000 a year. After that, there is no tax on the amount of money above the $28,000. These are precisely the people who need exemptions! People earning more than $28,000 certainly need more privileges than they already possess!
This bill might have been written by the Canadian Manufacturers Association or by the chamber of commerce or even right here in the Rideau club. These are the people who would propose such legislation as this, in order to keep the workers in economic slavery. This is what the bill before us is designed to do-to deprive those already on a low rate of income of more and more of that income so that they will become economic slaves.
Dedication to hard work is perpetuated by various organizations. I think the minister must be reading the wrong books when he seeks to co-operate with these people and falls for the propaganda and drivel they have spouted over the last hundred years. In 1951 the chamber of commerce was urging us to work harder to produce more because our survival might depend upon how fast we could keep the wheels of industry turning in Canada. But for whose benefit did these people want the wheels of industry to turn faster? The minister goes along, making sure that the worker gets the work and that the money men get the money. This is what they call a 50-50 split.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We hear a good deal, also, about the nobility of work. Well, most of it, as 1 happen to know from 31 years in mining and smelting, is not noble. The only reason people work in mills and smelters is because they are forced to do so in order to feed their families. I heard a little story about this ennoblement of work. A very popular man in the United States, Bobby Kennedy, was campaigning in front of one of the filthy steel mills, shaking hands with the men coming out of the mill. One grizzled old veteran on his way out said, "I hear, sonny, you never worked a day in your fife." "Yes, sir," said Bobby, "1 never spent a day in my life in a place like this," and the veteran said, "Well, you haven't missed a God damned thing." That is what is going on in the mills and smelters on this continent, Mr. Speaker: You haven't missed a thing.
Recently a study was made of the taxation system in Canada. Mr. Carter, I believe a very wise and noble person, presented a
Income Tax Act
report wherein he said that the tax system in Canada is one of the most unfair systems ever devised, and that 5 per cent of the people receive privileges at the expense of the other 95 per cent. I have a good idea who these 5 per cent of the privileged people are.
We talk about people's capitalism, and we are supposed to be receiving some of the benefits of that capitalism. But you and I, Mr. Speaker, know that only 10 per cent of the people own shares in corporations. If you deduct the people like myself who own one share, and people who own two shares like my friends, you will find that 2 per cent of the people control 98 per cent of the corporations, yet all our legislation seems designed to protect these 2 per cent who have us by the throat.
That is probably the reason why we do not have a capital gains tax in Canada. The only nation in the western world without a capital gains tax is this great country of ours. This generates people like Viola MacMillan and Mr. Justice Landreville who make great gobs of money, and it is all tax free. There is no justification for that type of exemption. It is not necessary.
There is another type of person who reaps benefit from our income tax legislation, and the minister could have done a favour to Canada if he had plugged this particular loophole. In this regard I speak of stock options given to members of boards of directors. It is a well known fact that people on the boards of various companies do not get an annual raise in pay because, as salary, it would be taxable. Instead, a means has been devised whereby they get a raise every year without having to pay their proper tax on it. It is known as a stock option.
These people are given an option to purchase stock at a fixed and given price any time they wish during the year. When they see the stock rise they can exercise their option. If they have an option on 10,000 shares and the market is up $5 a share they can go through a paper transaction, buy the stock at their option price, sell it at the board price and make $50,000 with ten minutes work. This is tax free because it is known as a capital gain. Such a device places a greater burden on people who make their living through wages alone, and these people comprise the vast majority of the population.
This bill rubs a little salt into the wound by charging the working man a 5 per cent increase on his payable taxes. Does anybody doubt where this increase, collected from the

February 6, 1968
Income Tax Act
lower income worker, is going? It is going back to the corporations to repay them that refundable portion of tax taken off them two years ago. Further, it is going to pay them that back at 5 per cent interest. The money to be taken out of the workingman's pocket is to be given to the corporations in repayment for that refundable tax.
Never in my experience has a government come to me and said, "Will you lend me some money for two years and I will pay it back to you at 5 per cent interest." But this is precisely what the government is doing in this bill. The government has to refund the corporation tax, and to do so it is getting the money from the workingman.
For many years the resource industry has had a privileged position in our tax structure. Depletion allowances are provided for the oil and mining industry. If these allowances had been eliminated the federal treasury could have picked up an extra $150 million in the past year, money which could have paid the corporation refundable tax without necessitating this 5 per cent income surtax on wage earners.
There is another vicious exemption in our tax structure, namely the three year tax exemption given to new mines. I know of this exemption quite well, coming from the mining community of Sudbury where we have debated it long and hard over the past 15 or 20 years. We have come to the conclusion that this is a direct steal on the part of the mining companies. Those companies must have exercised a direct influence on this and previous governments. The law providing that exemption was passed 40 years ago, when mining was a dangerous, speculative game. Since there was such a high risk involved it was necessary to encourage mining companies; but things have changed in the last 40 years. People do not sink mining shafts in the ground any more unless they know in advance what tonnage of ore lies underneath, what its percentage of metal is, and what return they will get on their investment. But even though advances in technical knowledge have eliminated the high risk involved, the legislation has not been changed for 40 years. There is no justification for mining companies to enjoy this three year tax exemption at present. Today when companies undertake to develop an ore body they plan its development very carefully so that by the end of the three year period the ore is raped just about clean. When the time comes for them to pay taxes there is no ore left in the ground. Then

they move on to another ore body and repeat the process.
Insurance and finance companies are also enjoying a privileged status under our tax system. Despite revenues of $90 million, after paying dividends, policy fees and everything else, these companies pay tax on only $5 million of that, and last year our federal treasury collected only $2 million. If these companies lost their privileged position our treasury could have picked up $77 million, which would have gone a long way to offset the deficit financing that seems to be the rule at present.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
There is another problem staring us in the face; that is the problem of supplying housing for our people. Part of the blame for the high cost of housing has been placed on the high cost of land. The reason for the high cost of land is that there are people who, with design, grab large tracts of land in areas where they know development will take place. After someone has paid the cost of installing sewers, services and roads all around this land in an area of 10, 20 or 100 acres the land value rises and the speculators come in and sell this land sometimes at a hundred fold profit over what they had paid for it. The people who need a bit of land in that particular community have no choice but to pay the price the speculator demands. The speculators of course do not have to pay income tax because this is called a capital gain.
If these transactions were not considered capital gains, more revenue would be collected for the treasury and land would be cheaper for the people who need to buy it in order to build a house. Without the capital gains provision, there would not be very much incentive for people like E. P. Taylor, who grabbed all of the township land near Malton airport, to go out and make this kind of a deal. In this case a person would not have to pay $10,000 or $12,000 for a 50 foot by 100 foot piece of land on which to build a home. It is a crying shame that land speculators are able to do this, without making a one penny contribution to the federal treasury. It is a complete and utter steal; it is banditry.
The corporations have done well for themselves through their control and direction of the old line parties. They have always held a privileged position in respect of travel and entertainment. Many people in the upper echelons in this country are living on their expense accounts. This expense account living
February 6, 1968

includes T-bone steaks, trips to Miami and California, or trips to Hawaii. So long as they make a phone call when they get there they can call it a business trip and it is tax free; it is charged out to the corporation. I am sure we all know of instances where people have taken their families along on such trips, where golf club dues are charged as a business expense, or where Christmas parties complete with T-bone steaks and booze are held in the board rooms. This is a direct charge on the people, who have to pay their full share of income tax because no provision is made for them.
There is no place on the income tax form for the average ordinary man where he can make any claim for entertainment expenses. When he entertains, he does so with the dollar on which he has already paid tax; But the privileged few do not have to do this. People who make money on the stock market are also exempt from taxation. There is no reason to my mind why a buck is not called a buck every time you see it. But we have the speculative dollar, the capital gains dollar and the earned dollar. The earned dollar takes the beating. There is the long dollar and the short dollar. They both look the same to me, except that I know one of them has a tax levied on it and the other has not.
Mr. Carter recommended redistribution of the entire tax burden. If this had been done the federal treasury could have counted on $523 million more in taxation in the past year. If there is a shortage of funds, I see no reason why those people who have the ability to pay are not charged this extra amount. Out of the $523 million, $270 million would have come from foreign corporations. This would have gone a long way toward buying back Canada.
The Prime Minister in his great pronouncement said that his goal in life is to try to buy Canada back, or gain control of our economy. What better way could this be done than by taxing these corporations $270 million more than they are paying now. The poor fellow who must pay a tax on all his earned income has very few exemptions. He can deduct his union dues of $60 a year, and $100 for general expenses if he happens to have a hospital bill, and so on. Other than that, however, he has no way in which he may deduct from his wages those items which he must purchase in order to earn his living. We know that every man in business or the professions who buys rubber bands, pen nibs, pencils and other articles deducts all these items because they have
Income Tax Act
been purchased in order to help him carry on his business. No matter how small the item, it finds its way on to the income tax form as a tax deduction.
Let us compare this situation with the situation of the man who must labour for wages, particularly in the industry in which I was employed. He cannot deduct any item, even though it is necessary in his employment. He must provide himself with a hard hat which costs $11. He must provide himself with safety boots which cost $14. He must have gloves with an iron protector on the back. He must have spats on. He must have overalls and rainwear. This man must provide himself with all sorts of safety equipment, plus his tool bag. When he is dressed up he has probably spent $500 in order to be prepared to do his first day's work. He cannot deduct any of that $500 from his income tax. I say it is a disgrace that this situation should exist. These people who must buy these things as a condition of employment should be allowed to deduct such items as an expense in respect of their income tax.
This reminds me of an occasion when a group of people with whom I was employed were working in 40 below zero weather. They were up on a hill installing a transformer. The superintendent asked them how they could stay out in this weather, and one of them replied "There is nothing to it, if you spend $400 on clothes and bullet-proof underwear". There is no deduction for that. I hope that the next time the minister brings in an amendment to the Income Tax Act he will show some compassion for the people who have created the wealth which permits these other people to float around in the enjoyment of an expense account living.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)

Now, Mr. Speaker, after greeting these gentlemen I must deal with the bill before the house wherein are announced increases in taxes and income tax, by the following introductory words:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
Income tax and taxes are therefore increased. The Queen, on the advice of her ministers, decides to increase taxes.
Mr. Speaker, that is probably why the Liberals have said:	Let us get rid of the
monarchy, since the Queen is the one who enacts increases in income tax and other taxes. That is the case, and I should like to protest against those increases.
In his speech on November 30 last, the hon. Minister of Finance said, while announcing the tax increase: We need additional revenue and to this end we must find other sources of revenue. The country is developing. Productivity must increase. Public works must expand in order to alleviate unemployment. Additional sources of revenue are then needed.
As reported at page 4908 of Hansard for November 30, 1967, the Minister of Finance decreed an income tax increase which is already in force although it has yet to be passed. That might be the reason why Her Majesty decrees and when she does we start paying on the very same day, even if that decree is passed two or three months later by parliament. It is as if parliament had nothing to say in the matter. Her Majesty has decreed; that is the end of it and we start paying right away. Parliament will vote when it wants to, it does not matter; taxes are collected as soon as Her Majesty has so decreed.
In any event the Minister of Finance said on November 30 and I quote:
My officials estimate that this surtax will increase our revenues in the fiscal year 1968-69 by $185 million; the effect on the current year will be to increase our revenues by approximately $25 million.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance says that he needs $25 million, and he levies a surtax. If he needs that sum, very well, but I submit that he should take it elsewhere than in the pockets of Canadian citizens who are already overtaxed and whose income tax is

already very high. Let us find another source of income. I found one, and I make a suggestion to that effect to the minister, because-

No. Mr. Speaker, I will leave this kind of joking to the hon. member for Chicoutimi, and I will continue to be serious.
Mr. Speaker, can we imagine that the Minister of Finance who needs $25 million should overtax the Canadian public to get it. I found in the estimates of the minister another source of revenue which would enable him to save $26 million, which is a little more than the amount he needs.
In fact, on page 318 of the estimates of National Defence for the current year, I note that the Minister of Finance has decided to purchase bombs for an amount of $26 million, that is $1 million more than the $25 million which he wants to collect from the Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that Canada does not need bombs at the present time, especially since last year the government had bought some for $21 million. Now the bombs bought last year have never been used. I do not remember that they were dropped on somebody, that we have declared the war on the United States or on Europe to drop $21 million worth of bombs or that, without being aware of it, we are involved in the Viet Nam war.
So, last year, we bought $21 million worth of bombs. We still have them. Very well, let us keep them. There is no need to buy another $26 million worth this year. Let us stop buying bombs and we shall have the $25 million the minister needs to balance his budget, since he says himself, in Hansard of November 30, 1967, that this surtax will bring in $25 million for the current year.
Mr. Speaker, I say again to the Minister of Finance, if he needs $25 million, the solution does not lie in taking that amount from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers, who are already overtaxed, but in practising economy where this can be done, and I suggest that the place where savings can be made is when buying bombs, since a sum of $26 million is allocated to that. There may be other areas where savings can also be realized. I know that, during the present fiscal year, the Department of National Defence will spend $21 million for telephone calls. Let them stop making long-distance calls. After all, we are
February G, 1968

not at war and we can save money in this way.
Moreover, we could try to make our money work for peace. Unemployment is rising, Mr. Speaker. In the city of Montreal itself, a week ago, there were approximately 65,000 unemployed, a continual increase over the number of unemployed last year. Meanwhile, millions of dollars earned through hard work and effort by the Canadian taxpayers and taken away from them are being spent on telephone calls or on bombs. Since this goes on from year to year, we must have accumulated quite a few bombs since the last world war, for you can buy quite a lot for $26 million.
We are also buying tanks and armoured cars; we spent $15 million on them. This year, the amount of $61 million has been appropriated for the purchase of warships and $95 million for the purchase of aircraft. Mr. Speaker, I submit such purchases are not urgent. What is urgent is to leave to Canadians the little money they have managed to earn with their salaries. I wonder what we could do to have the Minister of Finance understand that his responsibilities not only involve taxation but the setting up of an economic system which will help the Canadian people as a whole instead of being a nuisance.
Since the new Minister of Finance has been in office, many new taxes have been levied. These are putting a heavy burden on the Canadian taxpayers, but the minister does not call a halt, he is still increasing taxes. He has become "the hon. federal Minister of Taxes".
Every year, even twice a year, for two or three years now, he has been introducing two budgets a year and raising taxes. Mr. Speaker, I should like to protest against that increase. Personally, I shall vote against it. I object to it because the collection of those taxes started even before the legislation was passed by parliament and I say to myself: If hon. members are conscientious and honest, they will vote against it and the bill will not be passed. Each member represents some electors, citizens who are tired of paying taxes. He must therefore vote against that unjustified tax increase whatever his political allegiance.
The minister tells us that this surcharge will bring in $25 million which is $1 million less than the cost of the bombs which we are going to buy in the same year. Why not stop buying bombs? That is what each and every member should understand. The interest of the voters demands that we stop buying bombs instead of increasing taxes by 5 per
Income Tax Act
cent. It is always 1 per cent, 3 per cent, 5 per cent; taxes always go up and we do not know where this will stop.
Therefore, I strongly urge the members of all parties to vote against this bill so that this income tax increase will not come into force and Canadian citizens can breathe a bit more freely.

I should like to suggest certain guiding principles which I believe should be a part of our basic thinking:
1.	We must realize that long-term economic growth in real terms can be achieved not with but only without inflation.
2.	We must strive for an achievable rate of relatively constant growth-not a succession of sharp ups and downs.
3.	We must not, as we come out of a recession, seek to force the economy into a quick boom which can later injure our long run capacity to produce.
4.	We must put major reliance upon the private sector of the economy to increase production.
5.	We must give maximum free rein to incentive to save, to work, to produce, to invest.
6.	We must maintain the priceless incentive of confidence in the value of money.
7.	We must achieve a budget that is in balance, or better, during periods of high level activity.
8.	We must be willing to seek out the impediments to growth in our economy whether these are found in traditional business practices, in organized labour, in government subsidy programs, or in any other area.
9.	We must encourage the inventiveness and research necessary for new products, new jobs and improved living standards in a growing economy.
10.	We must accept the imposition of discipline and prudent responsibility.
11.	We must not passively allow either inflation or deflation to run its course.
12.	We must-and by "we" I mean businessmen, workers, investors, and not only officials of government-make our day to day decisions with the welfare of the whole in mind, and not merely the advantage of the moment for some narrow segment.
13.	Finally, we must have confidence-and this confidence, I have deep faith, is well justified- that the American people are wise enough and perceptive enough to support the principles which can leave for your children and mine an America not ravaged by economic turmoil, but full of strength and growth and hope.

I recently read with interest representations made to the federal government by chambers of commerce, labour organizations, agricultural organizations and municipalities, all of which indicate a measure of self-interest, instead of considering the problem as a whole. The brief of the chambers of commerce dealt with depreciation allowances and exemptions for certain industries, such as the resource industries and so on.
The brief submitted by organized labour dealt with the question of expense accounts, something that has been very much abused in the past. I have before me an article that appeared in an issue of the Star Weekly headed "The expense account gap", one paragraph of which reads:
It involves plugging the gaping loopholes in tax deductions allowed for entertainment and travelling expenses supposedly incurred for business reasons. The language of the present laws is so loose and imprecise that it has encouraged the creation of a privileged class which uses the loopholes to live high off the hog, writing off anything from country club membership fees to chartered limousines as "business expenses".
For the information of the minister I should like to relate an interesting personal experience I had last year in this respect. I was travelling by train from Vancouver to the Kootenays and there was a group of travellers on the train. One of them was supposed to visit a number of towns in the Kootenays-Nelson, Cranbrook, Fernie-and in my presence he quite openly admitted that he was going to go to Nelson but was not going to visit these other towns at all. Instead he was going to phone the storekeepers concerned from Nelson and take their orders; but he said: "Of course, I shall charge the usual expenses to my account just as if I had gone to those towns, stayed in hotels and incurred the usual expenses".
I am not sure that this sort of thing has been corrected to date by any means. It is something that needs watching very closely. I

can well understand organized labour criticizing the expense account racket, as they see it, when they are denied certain exemptions for expenses travelling to work, for the type of clothing referred to by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Germa), and other things of that nature.

The representations to the federal government made by the municipalities have dealt generally with urging more grants to municipalities in lieu of taxation on federal buildings in the municipalities, and also the need for social capital in connection with various undertakings. I have before me a copy of "The Listening Post" which is published by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. According to this, their brief called attention to these basic needs:
, (1) long-term federal loans at favourable rates of interest in order to finance projects which are primarily self-liquidating and essential to community development, such as urban roads, bridges and transit facilities, sewers, water supply, recreation space, and the acquisition of land for redevelopment:
(2)	grants on a more adequate scale toward the costs of hospitals, schools and other community services which are essential but non-self-liquidating;
(3)	continued and expanded grant assistance for employment-creating municipal works, to accelerate re-employment and to provide constructive work in the winter seasons.
The brief then dealt with a municipal development bank and the need for a new housing policy at that date, a matter we are still dealing with, in view of the housing crisis in Canada at the present time. The problem of finance and taxation has, shall I say, been dealt with on a piecemeal basis by all of the interests concerned, each one naturally looking after its own personal interest. It indicates a piecemeal approach to a very serious problem facing the country at this time. It also indicates that there is no over-all set of principles with which to approach the policy of taxation, Mr. Speaker. It indicates a natural self interest of individuals, and that we have treated this subject in a segmented way instead of adhering to the over-all philosophy that taxation should be on the basis of one's ability to pay.

I suggest that for so many in this country at this time to be ignorant of the principles of

taxation, is deplorable. Our people are ignorant of the financial principles on which the present government bases its taxation. I suggest to the minister that here is an opportunity for the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue to carry out an educational campaign; here is an opportunity for brochures, pamphlets, literature-[DOT] or whatever you want to call it-to be issued to our farmers, industrialists or workingmen to explain the policy behind the government's program, the reasons for certain types of taxation, why the government has come to certain conclusions, and so on.
I think it is imperative to educate the Canadian people and to let them learn the basis of taxation as applied by this government. In that way our people will have a better understanding of the principles of taxation and in the future will be able more and more to appreciate our problems, shall I say, in total rather than on the basis of self interest, as happens at the present time. I think there is an opportunity here for the Departments of Finance and National Revenue to inform and to educate the Canadian people with respect to the principles of taxation and the policies pursued by this government. Such knowledge would be useful because it would help our people to appreciate policy and it would help our taxpayers to have a proper understanding of the law as it is applied at the present time. On that basis the government might be able to consider a more rational and, shall I say, principled approach to taxation in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago, on
November 17 last to be exact, I addressed a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) in these words, as they appear at page 4393 of Hansard for that day:
In view of the fact that many persons who have been sentenced to life imprisonment have been paroled after serving fewer than ten years, and in view of the fact that the length of time in prison before parole is determined by the governor in council, will the government reconsider the case of a parole for Steven Truscott?

The Solicitor General in his reply indicated that the statistics to which I was referring applied to a time before changes had been made in the regulations under the Parole Act. He therefore felt nothing could be done to meet my request. At that time I posted this question for one of these adjournment debates.
I have no hesitation in appealing once again to the Solicitor General, on behalf of this young man Steven Truscott, who is serving a life sentence at Collin's Bay penitentiary. Indeed I have no hesitation in asking for special consideration for this young man. I do not intend to go into all of the facts relating to this case, but may I point out, as we all know, that the last time a decision was taken in respect of him it was a decision taken by the Supreme Court of Canada, which was not unanimous. Granted that only one of their lordships differed from the others, but it is still a recognized principle in this country that a person is not guilty of murder unless there is a unanimous decision.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I recognize that this was not a trial in the normal sense, but I suggest to the government that the fact that at least one Supreme Court justice had some doubt about this case, and thought that at least there should be a new trial, does warrant asking for special consideration for this young man. My own position is quite clear. Thanks to the Solicitor General and the Commissioner of Penitentiaries, I have had the opportunity on two occasions of visiting Steven Truscott at Collin's Bay penitentiary. On the basis of those visits and the studies I have made of the entire history of this case, I feel there has been a miscarriage of justice. Therefore, it does seem to me that one is justified in asking for special consideration.
But even apart from all that, I think it is a matter of record that this young man's years in prison-they are now nearly nine-have been as near perfect as a prisoner's record could be. I believe that on that basis special consideration should be given to the request that he be paroled before any more of his fife is spent behind bars.
When I have urged that this be done, the Solicitor General has replied that the parole board is governed by the regulations under the Parole Act. He has pointed out to me that those regulations have been changed in recent years and that it is not now possible to release after seven or eight years a person sentenced to imprisonment for life, as used to
February 6, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion be the case. But I point out to the Solicitor General that the regulations which govern the operations of the parole board are regulations brought into effect by the governor in council.
The minimum period of time, the ten year minimum that seems to stand in our way in this respect, is not in the act. That ten year minimum is in the regulations, put there by the governor in council. I submit that precisely because this case has had special consideration, has been reviewed by the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada, it would be appropriate for the government to take another look at those regulations with respect to this case.
I would not object if the government asked the parole board whether its members thought the case should be given special attention. But it seems to me that since the whole question of the length of time that must be served as a minimum is one that is determined by the governor in council, in other words by the cabinet, it is appropriate to ask the cabinet to review this case.
I recognize that this young man's ten year period in prison will be reached about the middle of 1969. That does not sound very far off, but in the case of a young man who has spent this length of time in jail for a crime that some of us think he did not commit, and when it is clear that there has been exemplary conduct in prison, it seems to me to warrant special consideration being given to the case.
I know of the sympathy of the Solicitor General in this respect. I think it was largely due to his interest in the case that the Supreme Court review was made a year or so ago. I hope that he will follow it through by taking another look at the possibility of this young man being given a parole without having to serve the full ten years set out in the regulations passed by the governor in council. I thank the Solicitor General for being here tonight to deal with this question. I look forward, hopefully, to a sympathetic reply.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to thank the hon. member for his patience in waiting for an evening that was convenient to me to be present in the house to deal with his question. I wish also to say that the hon. member's interest in this case is most commendable. Without reflecting in the slightest upon the conduct of this young inmate, I feel I ought not to make any comment on that aspect of the case.
[Mr, Knowles.)
I agree that the response to a like term of imprisonment varies as between one individual and another. Unfortunately, according to the present state of knowledge, decisions regarding the appropriate moment to release a prisoner cannot be made with computer-like accuracy. In 1964 those charged with the responsibility of protecting society decided that the National Parole Board shall not recommend a parole in the case of a person who is serving a commuted death sentence until that person shall have served at least ten years of imprisonment. This order in council was undoubtedly in the minds of many hon. members at the time the house approved the recent bill on capital punishment.
I regret to advise the hon. member that I expect that the ten year period would be continued at least during the five year life of this experimental bill. The only assurance I can give the hon. member is that the National Parole Board will consider the application in sufficient time before the expiration of the ten year period, so that if it receives favourable consideration it will be in the hands of the solicitor general of the day on June 11, 1969, which is the first day on which the governor in council could receive a favourable recommendation.

Mr. Speaker, I
should like to discuss tonight the program of occupational training of adults, such as the one proposed in the house on January 19, 1967 by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, a policy which was intended for those in the uneconomic regions of our country who wish to upgrade their education. In his statement on that date, which is contained in information bulletin No. 1, the minister admitted that his department had very little documentation on the problem of how to encourage these unemployed persons to take advantage of courses preparing them for a new job. This admission has caused much unrest in these regions, because of the discrimination which was caused through lack of sufficient knowledge.

It seems to me that this problem has not been sufficiently studied. As a result thousands of people in this country are now discriminated against. These are people who are now unemployed and could improve their education by taking one of these occupational training courses for adults.
I should like to point out that in many regions of Canada, and specifically in my riding, there are many people who attended courses during the 1966-67 period and were still at school on March 31, 1967. Because of this fact they qualify to attend new courses commencing this year. I believe that during this period it was sufficiently proven that many of the people who attended these courses should never have qualified for them, but it seems that they were never classified as a result of any investigation. This year those who qualified were primarily those who were at school on March 31, 1967. Even though they were not qualified to take a course the previous year, because they were at school on March 31, 1967 they qualified for a course this year.
This has meant that thousands of people will this year be deprived of a course. I say thousands because at one centre in my riding alone over 800 people who qualified for a course were turned down owing to lack of space. I blame this situation on the government because they did not sufficiently study this pilot project without even trying to assess the number of people who would qualify for a course.
This has meant that the people who would have qualified now have to draw unemployment insurance and sit at home, instead of

maintopic: HOUSING-VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION OF HOME FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
HOUSING-VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION OF HOME FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 2 1 asked the President of the Treasury Board, the minister who reports for central mortgage and housing, the following question as reported on page 6291 of Hansard:
In view of the minister's interest in getting the best use of the money available for housing, can he inform the house why Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has awarded a contract for the construction of a 19 storey senior citizens home in Vancouver which provides for higher costs and fewer units than other proposals submitted for the same project?
The approximate cost of this project, which is to be located in the west end of Vancouver, is about $1,600,000. Seventy five per cent of this amount will be paid by the federal government and 25 per cent by the provincial government. The city of Vancouver will pay 12J per cent of the operating losses. The federal involvement here is about $1,200,000. Actually it is a bit more than that.
Instead of preparing plans and calling for tenders, the government invited architects and developers to submit design proposals. A committee which included representatives of the city of Vancouver, the province of British Columbia and C.M.H.C. studied these proposals and made a recommendation.
What I have to say should not be taken as a reflection on the abilities or competence of any architects or builders. I assume they are all capable of designing sound buildings of good appearance. Nor does it matter to me, personally, which firm gets a contract. What does matter at this time of severe housing shortage and high money cost is that good accommodation be provided at the lowest possible price.
I want to draw some comparisons between the proposal which was accepted and one proposal which was not accepted. The proposal which was accepted has 210 units; the other one I referred to has 233 units. The difference there is 23 units, and this is particularly important in this section of Vancouver, since so many elderly people live in sub-standard accommodation.

DEBATES	February 6. 196k
The size of each apartment in the project which was picked by the committee is about 311 square feet; the units in the other proposal come to approximately 325 square feet, and this is not very much space to live in. The average monthly rental for accommodation in the building selected would be $92 and, in the other, $85. A difference of $7 a month may not appear to be very high, but to some people, those who are living on pensions, it is an important consideration. The total cost of the two projects did not differ greatly-$1,669,131 for the winning proposal as against $1,647,724 for the other to which I have referred. However, since there are fewer units in the proposal selected, the actual cost per unit is considerably higher, and extended over the life of the building, say 50 years, the difference would be great. This means that heavier subsidies will be required because of the higher rentals under the first proposal.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I wish now to read a letter from the president of the Vancouver Housing Association addressed to the council of the city of Vancouver and dated January 12, 1968. It states:
Dear Sirs:
I have been puzzled by the decision of city council to accept a tender for a public housing project for senior citizens in the west end which was very appreciably higher in cost (well over 10 per cent per suite of comparable size) and which contained fewer units than the lowest bid.
One of our members, who has had considerable experience in the construction of senior citizens housing, has studied the plans submitted by the low bidder and, while he did not feel competent to express an opinion on the architectural and constructional features of the project, he considered that so far as the liveability of the units was concerned the plans provided good accommodation at a reasonable cost.
In the circumstances, may I suggest that for the benefit of the taxpayer who will have to foot the extra bill a detailed explanation be given as to the reasons for the selection of the higher tender.
May I, at the same time, suggest that future selection committees appointed to consider plans submitted should include persons with extensive personal knowledge of the needs of elderly people and with firsthand experience in public housing management.
Yours very truly,
Vancouver Housing Association
The letter is signed by Mrs. C. McAllister, president of the association.
There is one further point I should like to mention. The proposal which was not selected did provide on the ground floor suites for physically handicapped persons, obviously a desirable feature. The proposal selected by the committee did not include this feature in
February 6, 1968	COMMONS
its original presentation, though I believe there have been some changes in the plans since that time. The question I should like to have answered is this: Why, at a time of acute housing shortage and shortage of money, was a selection made which provided fewer and smaller units at a higher cost? It seems to me there is considerable waste here.

I think that in matters of this kind we could all find ourselves in disagreement. I will say that this has been a co-operative effort. I should like to read an answer which has been prepared very thoughtfully, and I am able to do so because the hon. member was good enough to word his question in such a way that it was quite evident which aspects of the subject he had in mind.
The senior citizens housing project to be located in the west end of Vancouver is being developed at the request of the city of Vancouver under the federal-provincial partnership provisions of the National Housing Act. To meet the city's request, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, on behalf of the partnership, called for proposals to be made by builders for the construction of approximately 200 units.
Under the terms of the partnership arrangement, proposals submitted by builders were to be judged by a review committee composed of provincial and corporation representatives as well as the city's director of planning and a local architect representing
DEBATES	6455
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the provincial architectural institute. Prospective proponents were advised that the review committee was required to judge proposals on the quality of planning and design, economy of maintenance and the amount of the bids.
Seven developers submitted bona fide proposals ranging in quality and price from $7,072 to $14,207 a unit. The review committee unanimously recommended acceptance of a proposal submitted by Frank Stanzl Construction Limited at a price of $7,910 a unit, as it considered that the over-all quality of design of this proposal, comprising 211 units, was of a high standard and, on balance, best met the objectives and conditions provided for in the call. The city, the province and the corporation endorsed the committee's recommendations. As a result, a contract was awarded to the proponent selected by the committee. An announcement to this effect was made last week.
I would just like to add, Mr. Speaker, that I think there is always room for disagreement in this sort of operation, but I would also like to stress the fact that it was a co-operative effort, an effort to do something by way of senior citizens housing in Vancouver, and I suggest the people represented by the city, the province and the architectural institute, as well as C.M.H.C., might be just as well qualified to judge the design as those who have disagreed with the awarding of the contract.
